I think decriminalization of personal drug use is likely justified, though the case is stronger for some substances than others.

The core issue is that criminalization causes substantial harms that often exceed those from the drugs themselves: mass incarceration, criminal records that destroy employment prospects, incentives for violent drug markets, and erosion of trust between communities and police. These are well-documented consequences, not speculative.

Decriminalization (treating use as a public health matter rather than criminal) doesn't mean endorsing drug use—it means recognizing that criminal penalties are a blunt instrument that generates collateral damage. Portugal's 20-year decriminalization experiment shows this can work: drug use rates didn't spike, overdose deaths fell, and treatment engagement improved.

I'm less convinced by arguments for full legalization across all substances, since some (like methamphetamine) have particularly severe addiction profiles and social costs that might warrant continued restrictions on supply. But personal possession shouldn't trigger criminal prosecution.

The strongest counterargument—that this signals permissiveness and increases use—has limited empirical support. Most people don't use hard drugs regardless of legal status; those struggling with addiction respond better to health interventions than punishment.

My core values here are reducing unnecessary suffering and respecting human dignity. Mass incarceration for drug possession fails both tests. A public health approach better serves these principles while remaining pragmatic about genuine harms.
